title: Science of Learning Alliance (SoLA) Explicit Maths Conference
author: Sue Knight
summary: This is Part 3 of a four-part conference-reflection series by Sue Knight, School Improvement Lead at Teach Well, recounting ten days spent across two Australian education conferences and school visits. The central argument is that sustainable school improvement rests less on any single initiative than on developing middle leaders who bridge principals and classroom teachers, backed by high-quality, centrally planned curriculum materials that free teachers' intellectual effort for delivery rather than resource creation from scratch. Knight synthesizes conference takeaways from several speakers: Liana McCurry on why high-performing mathematics systems favor rigorous, textbook-supported curricula and early intervention; Dr Reid Smith on the evidentiary case for high-quality instructional materials and 'intellectual preparation'; and Toni Hatten-Roberts and Bruno Reddy on ambitious, fluency-focused mathematics instruction grounded in working-memory research. Threaded through the piece are sixteen numbered 'tips' distilling the conference experience into actionable school-improvement guidance, spanning curriculum expertise, middle-leadership development, and awareness of education policy history. The piece reads as a practitioner's field report addressed to principals and instructional leaders rather than a research paper for classroom teachers.
points: Argues school improvement depends on a minimum viable leadership team - a principal, at least one strong middle leader, and two committed teachers per roughly 250 students - and recommends building middle-leadership capacity deliberately through coaching and protected time to lead.

Cites Grattan Institute research that pre-planned, high-quality instructional materials free teachers to focus on the 'how' of delivery and adaptation rather than building resources from scratch, provided schools also budget real intellectual-preparation time.
Supplies concrete numeric benchmarks for maths fluency (40 digits correct per minute; automatic fact recall well before Year 4) drawn from international curriculum comparisons.
Warns against over-scaffolding change: recommends limiting how many new curriculum initiatives a school introduces at once and slowing implementation to protect quality.
Urges leaders to study education policy and history to understand present constraints, then to make evidence-based decisions regardless of bureaucratic limitations.
quotes: In her presentation Liana referenced the enormous workload born by teachers when we are expected to read and interpret curriculum documents, sequence knowledge, create units of work and lesson plans, source or create assessments, and collate and respond to data, for upwards of six learning areas in a primary school as a generalist classroom teacher. Even working with a good team, that is a huge ask.
We are now at the stage where we have our curriculum planned. We are picking up units of work, looking over them as a team, tweaking and refining them and making them better.
Reid is a master communicator, calm and measured. Every so often you get a glimpse of the incredible intellect that drives his work.

Middle leaders sit in a very unique place between principal class and teachers, and often this is place of some tension. Teachers can't know all the challenges that principals face and the decisions they are making, and we, as principals, don't know what it is like to be teaching full-time in demanding and complex classrooms. Middle leaders have been key to every single successful school improvement initiative I have been a part of.

I have a theory that to build sustainable school improvement at a minimum you need a team of a principal, at least one gun middle leader, and two teachers, all with deep knowledge and an unfailing belief in the work. That's for a school of about 250 students. The ratio moves up and down depending on school size.
Just do the right thing. Make good decisions for your students, in your classroom, in your school, and in your system, based on evidence and research. No excuses.
